extracted.intended_audience: public relations counsel / PR practitioners / press agents
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for public relations professionals on evaluating public opinion, selecting media channels, and framing messages so they will be accepted by newspapers and other organs that help make public opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the public's a_priori judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: “Thus the public relations counsel has to consider the _a priori_ judgment of any public he deals with before counseling any step that would modify those things in which the public has an established belief.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before proposing persuasion tactics, audit the existing beliefs and assumptions of the target public; account for those settled attitudes when planning communications. Examine sources of established beliefs and avoid strategies that collide head-on with them without preparatory work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discredit old authorities or create new authorities
rubrics_metrics.description: “After examination of the sources of established beliefs, must either discredit the old authorities or create new authorities by making articulate a mass opinion against the old belief or in favor of the new.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If changing an accepted belief, do not simply attack the belief itself; instead undermine the credibility of the sources people trust or cultivate and publicize new, respected authorities and organized supporters to legitimize the new position.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid name-calling and direct denigration of beliefs
rubrics_metrics.description: “It is seldom effective to call names or to attempt to discredit the beliefs themselves.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid personal attacks on opponents or dismissive rhetoric; such tactics are counterproductive. Focus on evidence, new authorities, and framing that respects audience identity to reduce defensive backlash.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess whether public opinion is stubborn or malleable
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a divergence of opinion as to whether the public mind is malleable or stubborn—whether it is a passive or an active element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze topic- and audience-specific receptivity; some issues and publics are resistant (examples: re‑election despite press opposition) while others can be changed by persistent institutional effort (examples: woman suffrage, birth control, health education). Tailor strategy accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study and evaluate the channels that shape opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: “Many outside forces…parental influence, the school room, the press, motion pictures, advertising, magazines, lectures, the church, the radio.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map the relevant institutions and media that reach the target public; estimate their relative power and biases. Choose channels whose norms and audiences align with your objectives and where your message can be credibly received.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conform to the standards of the medium (what is 'fit to print')
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors must define what news ‘is fit to print’; Professor Bleyer: the only important limitations are decency and the rights of privacy; 'News is anything timely which is significant to newspaper readers….'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When pitching to a newspaper or other organ, respect its editorial standards—decency, readers' expectations, privacy rights, and sense of significance/timeliness. Tailor content format and selection to what the medium considers appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor message to the medium's and audience's moral limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: “A newspaper must adapt its pleading to its clients’ moral limitation just as the trial lawyer also must adapt _his_ pleading to the jury’s limitations.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust tone, imagery, and explicitness to the tastes and moral standards of the medium’s readership; doing otherwise risks rejection or backlash even if the argument is sound.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use existing channels strategically to gain expression
rubrics_metrics.description: “The counsel on public relations, desiring to obtain a hearing for any given cause, simply utilizes existent channels to obtain expression for the point of view he represents.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage established distribution networks (press, lectures, churches, film, radio, advertising) rather than attempting to invent wholly new ones; coordinate channels to reinforce the message.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enlist sponsors and group leaders to legitimize controversial content
rubrics_metrics.description: Example: producers of 'Damaged Goods' allowed group leaders and groups interested in education to come to the support of the production to avoid alienating public sentiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For sensitive or taboo topics, obtain endorsements and sponsorship from respected organizations or leaders to provide cover and legitimacy, rather than confronting public taboos directly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitor public feedback and use trial balloons
rubrics_metrics.description: Delegations maintained clipping bureaus and used public statements as 'trial balloons' to test popular reaction; officials used press reaction to guide strategy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continuously monitor media coverage and public reaction (clipping services, surveys, letters) and use tentative releases or signals to test receptivity before full commitment; adapt strategy based on feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for practical constraints on reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Constraints include advertisers' influence, the 'quality public' advertisers wish to reach, and the emotional difficulty of making certain facts interesting; also practical difficulty in uncovering news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that editorial choices are shaped by commercial and practical pressures—advertising concerns, audience composition, storytelling needs. Frame and package information so it is discoverable and compelling within those constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enlist established points of view to secure influence
rubrics_metrics.description: “The influence of any force…depends upon the success with which it is able to enlist established points of view.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build campaigns that resonate with prevailing attitudes and values where possible; anchoring new messages to familiar beliefs increases acceptance and reduces resistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be prepared to hold an independent line when required
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples (the two Baltimore Suns) show newspapers sometimes 'brave their public' and maintain consistent policies despite opposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When conviction and long-term strategy warrant it, maintain a consistent stance even if initially unpopular, understanding this is a high-risk approach that may succeed over time if well executed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid substituting personal attack for argument
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances where personal attack supersedes logic (e.g., tariff debate) are criticized; logical discussion should be based on sound economic, social and political value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep public arguments focused on substantive grounds (facts, policy impact) rather than impugning motives or character of opponents; appeals to reason are more defensible and less alienating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize 'logic-proof compartments' of audience expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: People may be open-minded in their field but dogmatic outside it; 'logic-proof compartments' mean expertise does not generalize across topics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Segment audiences by domain knowledge and avoid assuming competence across domains; tailor depth and type of evidence to the audience’s relevant expertise and likely receptivity.
